reference.source: Standard endocrinology reference texts and pituitary tumour consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: A pituitary adenoma of corticotroph lineage that stains for ACTH but does not cause clinical Cushing syndrome, so it behaves clinically like a non-functioning tumour
Diagnosis is usually made only on immunohistochemistry after surgery performed for mass effect, since preoperative biochemistry shows no overt cortisol excess
Presentation is typically with headache, visual field defects and hypopituitarism from a macroadenoma
These tumours are recognised as more aggressive than most non-functioning adenomas, with higher rates of cavernous sinus invasion, regrowth and recurrence
A minority can evolve to become clinically functioning and cause overt Cushing disease over time, so cortisol status needs ongoing review
Subtypes are described (including a densely and a sparsely granulated pattern), with the latter often behaving more aggressively
Because there is no hormone excess to target medically, close imaging surveillance and consideration of adjuvant radiotherapy for residual tumour are important
reference.pathophysiology: A silent corticotroph adenoma arises from pituitary corticotroph cells and expresses pro-opiomelanocortin and ACTH on immunostaining, yet fails to produce clinically significant hypercortisolism. This apparent silence is attributed to impaired processing or release of biologically active ACTH, so that despite the corticotroph phenotype the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is not clinically overactive. Clinical effects therefore stem from tumour bulk, causing optic chiasm compression, hypopituitarism and headache. The corticotroph lineage confers a more invasive and recurrence-prone behaviour than typical gonadotroph non-functioning adenomas, and dedifferentiation can occasionally lead to later hormone activation and overt Cushing disease.
additionalDifferentials: Overt corticotroph adenoma causing Cushing disease
additionalInvestigations: Pituitary MRI to assess size, invasion and suprasellar extension
Postoperative immunohistochemistry for ACTH and corticotroph transcription factors to establish lineage
Screening for subclinical or emerging cortisol excess (e.g. late-night salivary cortisol, dexamethasone suppression, 24-hour urinary free cortisol)
Full anterior pituitary hormone profile to detect hypopituitarism
Formal visual field testing when the chiasm is threatened
Serial imaging surveillance for regrowth given the higher recurrence risk
redFlags: Rapid tumour regrowth or cavernous sinus invasion on follow-up imaging
Development of clinical or biochemical Cushing syndrome indicating transformation to a functioning tumour
Progressive visual field loss from chiasmal compression
Pituitary apoplexy with acute headache and ophthalmoplegia
reference.prognosis: These tumours carry a higher risk of invasion, incomplete resection and recurrence than most non-functioning adenomas, so long-term outcomes are less favourable and lifelong surveillance is essential; a subset progresses to overt Cushing disease, and residual disease may need radiotherapy.
pitfalls: Assuming a non-functioning adenoma will behave indolently and under-monitoring for recurrence
Failing to reassess cortisol status over time and missing evolution into Cushing disease
Not obtaining corticotroph immunostaining, thereby misclassifying the tumour
Overlooking hypopituitarism, particularly cortisol deficiency, in the perioperative period
references: WHO classification and consensus guidance on pituitary adenomas
management: Transsphenoidal surgical resection is the mainstay, relieving mass effect on the optic chiasm and providing lineage-defining histology
Hormone replacement for any hypopituitarism (glucocorticoid, levothyroxine, sex steroids and growth hormone as indicated), with perioperative steroid cover
Radiotherapy, including stereotactic radiosurgery, for invasive, residual or recurrent tumour given the aggressive corticotroph behaviour
Long-term surveillance with serial pituitary MRI for regrowth and periodic biochemical screening for emerging cortisol excess and overt Cushing disease
Formal visual field monitoring while the chiasm is threatened
Coordinated pituitary multidisciplinary care with endocrinology, neurosurgery, radiation oncology and neuro-ophthalmology
Escalation to temozolomide for aggressive or progressive tumours behaving as pituitary carcinoma
